I have farmed this 8 mu of land in Quzhou for 35 years. My father grew wheat and maize here, and so do I. This is the North China Plain — wheat in winter, maize in summer, same fields, every year. The wheat is already in the ground from last October. Right now it is greening up, and I am getting ready for the busy spring work.

For my wheat, I will use the rotary tiller to prep the field before sowing every autumn — that is what I have always done. I buy improved wheat seeds from the county supply shop, varieties like Jimai or Shixin that resist rust. For fertilizer, I spread compound fertilizer as basal before sowing, then top-dress urea at jointing in March or April. I pump water from my well four times for wheat: before winter freeze, at greening, at jointing, and at heading. I spray pesticides about four times — herbicide in spring, insecticide for aphids, and fungicide if I see rust or powdery mildew. I expect about 1000 jin per mu, around 500 kg, if the weather cooperates.

For maize, I plant right after wheat harvest in June, direct-seeding into the wheat stubble with no tillage. That saves diesel and time, and I need to get the crop in fast before the rains. I always buy hybrid maize seed — Zhengdan or Denghai varieties — because the yield is much better than keeping my own seed. I put down compound fertilizer at sowing, and that is usually enough nitrogen for maize since the summer rains help. I irrigate maize twice from the well, mostly at flowering and grain filling if July is dry. I spray pesticides three times: herbicide after emergence, and insecticide for corn borer if I see it. I expect about 1100 jin per mu, roughly 550 kg.

My son works off-farm in town, so I manage most of the fieldwork myself. I do not experiment with new crops or fancy methods — I know what works on this land, and the grain station still buys wheat and maize at a stable price. That is enough for my family.
